\section[diēs]{diēs — the word you already know, now standing alone}

\label{lesson:LA-C28-dies}



\begin{quote}
You've used this word twice already without a lesson of its own — inside \emph{diēs Lūnae} and \emph{medius diēs}. Time to meet it directly.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: diēs — \textquotedblleft{}day\textquotedblright{}}
\textbf{Diēs} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{day}\textquotedblright{} — is a genuinely common, everyday Classical Latin word, not a rare or bookish one. You've already met it embedded in:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{diēs Lūnae} (\textquotedblleft{}Monday,\textquotedblright{} literally \textquotedblleft{}day of the Moon\textquotedblright{} — Chapter 5)
  \item \textbf{medius diēs} (\textquotedblleft{}noon,\textquotedblright{} literally \textquotedblleft{}mid-day\textquotedblright{} — Chapter 12)
\end{itemize}

Now it's the headword itself.

\begin{cousinweb}
Diēs has its own derivative, \textbf{diurnum} (\textquotedblleft{}daytime, daily\textquotedblright{}), which gives English \textbf{diurnal} directly — and, through French's \emph{jour}, \emph{journée}, and \emph{jornel} (all descendants of \emph{diurnum} in their own right), \textbf{journal} and \textbf{journey} as well (a \textquotedblleft{}journey\textquotedblright{} was originally \textquotedblleft{}a \textbf{day's} travel\textquotedblright{}). \textbf{Diary} takes a \textbf{separate} path: it comes from a \textbf{sibling} derivative of \emph{diēs}, \textbf{diārium} (\textquotedblleft{}daily allowance\textquotedblright{}), not from \emph{diurnum} itself — two related but distinct branches off the same root. Further out, a genuine \textbf{Proto-Indo-European} root, \emph{\textbf{*dyēws-}} (\textquotedblleft{}to shine, sky\textquotedblright{}), connects \emph{diēs} to Latin's own \textbf{deus} (\textquotedblleft{}god\textquotedblright{}) and to \textbf{Iuppiter} (Jupiter, literally \textquotedblleft{}sky-father\textquotedblright{}) — the same root that shines through the sky-god imagery of gods across the Indo-European world.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}diēs\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}day\textquotedblright{}
  \item where you've already met it — diēs Lūnae, medius diēs
  \item the English cousins — diurnal, diary, journal, journey
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where have you already met \textbf{diēs} twice before this lesson? (\textbf{Diēs Lūnae}, \textquotedblleft{}Monday\textquotedblright{}; \textbf{medius diēs}, \textquotedblleft{}noon.\textquotedblright{}) What English word comes from diēs's derivative \emph{diurnum} directly? (\textbf{Diurnal}.) What two words come through French descendants of \emph{diurnum} — \emph{jour}, \emph{journée}, \emph{jornel}? (\textbf{Journal, journey}.) Does \textbf{diary} also come from \emph{diurnum}? (\textbf{No} — a separate sibling derivative, \emph{diārium}, \textquotedblleft{}daily allowance.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
